chapters.title: Chapter 7: Sector Rotation and Applying Sector Analysis

lessons.title: Sector Rotation: How Leadership Shifts Across the Economic Cycle

body.text: No sector leads forever. The best performing sector of the last three years is often the worst performer of the next three, because leadership follows the economic cycle and because the market pays up for whatever is working until it is priced for perfection. Understanding rotation is less about predicting the next leader and more about not paying top price for the last one.

children.text: You have now analysed the major Indian sectors one by one. This final chapter puts them back together. This lesson covers how sector leadership shifts across an economic cycle, how to measure it, and the honest limits of using it as a retail investor.

The logic is simple once you connect Chapter 2 to everything since. In a downturn, defensive earnings hold up while cyclicals collapse. When rates are cut and recovery begins, the sectors that suffered most from high rates and weak demand rebound first. As the recovery matures, capital spending picks up. Late in the cycle, capacity gets tight and commodity prices rise. Then inflation forces rate hikes, growth slows, and money returns to defensives.

body.title: Which Sectors Typically Lead in Each Phase

events.title: Early recovery: rates falling, growth bottoming
events.description: Banks and NBFCs, autos, real estate, and consumer discretionary tend to lead. Lower rates revive loan demand and big-ticket purchases, and depressed cyclical earnings rebound from a low base.

events.title: Mid-cycle: growth broadening
events.description: Capital goods, engineering, cement, and industrials do well as companies and governments invest. Credit growth is healthy and asset quality is benign, which continues to support lenders.

events.title: Late cycle: capacity tight, inflation rising
events.description: Metals, mining, energy, and other commodity producers lead as prices rise. Margins peak, reported P/E ratios look deceptively low, and capacity expansions get announced.

events.title: Slowdown: rates rising, demand cooling
events.description: FMCG, pharma, utilities, and other defensives outperform, not usually by rising strongly but by falling less. Highly leveraged and richly valued companies de-rate the most.

events.title: The market moves before the data
events.description: Stock prices discount expected earnings, so sector leadership typically shifts months before GDP, inflation, or company results confirm the new phase.

body.title: Illustrative Relative Performance Across One Cycle (Index, Start = 100)

children.text: Notice the shape. Cyclicals deliver far more over the full cycle in this illustration, but they give back a large part of it in the slowdown, and an investor who bought them late in the cycle would have lost money while the defensive investor kept grinding forward. Both paths end higher. The experience of holding them is completely different, and most investors switch at exactly the wrong moment.

body.title: Indian examples of leadership changing hands

children.text: Recent Indian market history shows the pattern clearly, even if it never follows the textbook exactly. In 2020, pharma and IT led as the pandemic boosted demand for medicines and digital services while the domestic economy shut down. Through 2021 and into 2022, metals surged as global commodity prices spiked. In 2022, with the RBI hiking rates, public sector banks and capital goods led while IT fell sharply. Each shift looked obvious afterwards and was fiercely debated at the time.

One repeated feature is worth noting. In each case, the sector that led was one where earnings surprised on the upside relative to what the market had assumed, often starting from a low valuation. That is the real engine of rotation: not the economy in isolation, but the gap between what the market expected and what the sector delivered.

markDefs.definition: A simple ratio of a sector index to a broad market index. A rising ratio means the sector is outperforming the market; a falling ratio means it is lagging, regardless of whether prices are rising or falling overall.

children.text: The simplest way to see rotation is

: divide a sector index such as Nifty Bank or Nifty IT by the Nifty 50 and watch the trend. It removes the overall market direction and leaves only the question of whether this sector is gaining or losing ground.

body.latex: \text{Relative strength} = \frac{\text{Sector index}}{\text{Broad market index}} \qquad \text{Relative return} = \frac{1 + \text{Sector return}}{1 + \text{Market return}} - 1
body.caption: Relative strength tracks leadership; relative return measures how much a sector beat or lagged the market

body.title: How Much Did the Sector Really Beat the Market By?
body.prompt: Over a year, a sectoral index returns 25% while the Nifty 50 returns 10%. What is the sector's relative return, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 1.25 ÷ 1.10 = 1.136, so the sector outperformed by 13.6%, not the 15 percentage points a simple subtraction suggests. The distinction matters over multiple years, because relative returns compound just like absolute ones. If you had held this sector instead of an index fund, ₹1,00,000 would have become ₹1,25,000 rather than ₹1,10,000.

body.text: Sector rotation is far easier to see in hindsight than to trade in advance. By the time a phase is obvious in the data, prices have usually moved. Every switch also costs you brokerage, exit loads where applicable, and capital gains tax on the gains you book. Most retail investors rotate by buying whichever sector fund has the best three-year return, which is close to the opposite of what the strategy requires.

body.title: Buying Last Year's Winner
body.scenario: A colleague shows you a sectoral fund that has returned 42% a year over the last three years, far ahead of the Nifty 50. It is the top performing category on every fund website, and inflows into it have surged. The underlying sector's earnings are at record levels, its profit margins are well above their ten-year average, and several companies in it have announced large capacity expansions. He wants to invest a lump sum.
body.prompt: What would you point out, and how would you decide?
body.modelAnswer: Everything he has listed is backward looking and consistent with a late-cycle peak. Record earnings and margins far above the long-run average usually mean the spread is unusually wide, and industry-wide capacity expansion is the classic signal of supply arriving into a softer market, exactly the pattern from Chapters 2 and 6. Three-year return charts and surging inflows tell you the move has already happened and that sentiment is crowded. That does not automatically mean the sector will fall, but it does mean he would be buying at high expectations, high margins, and high valuations. Before deciding, check: the sector's current valuation against its own ten-year range, ideally on normalised earnings; whether margins are at peak or mid-cycle levels; the supply pipeline; and how much of his existing portfolio, including index and large cap funds, already has exposure to this sector. If he still wants exposure, staggering it over several months and sizing it as a small satellite position is far safer than a lump sum chasing the return chart.

body.title: Read the Phase
body.question: The RBI has started cutting rates after a long pause, GDP growth has bottomed out, bank asset quality is stable, and cyclical stocks trade below their historical average valuations. Based on the classic rotation map, which group would you expect to lead next?
body.explanation: This describes an early recovery phase: falling rates revive loan demand and big-ticket purchases funded by EMIs, so rate-sensitive sectors such as lenders, autos, and real estate typically lead. Defensives tend to lag in recoveries, and commodity producers usually lead later in the cycle when capacity tightens and prices rise. Remember, these are tendencies, not guarantees.

children.text: A Practical Alternative: Rebalancing Instead of Forecasting

There is a way to benefit from rotation without predicting it. Set target weights for sectors or funds, then rebalance periodically back to those targets. This mechanically trims whatever has run up and adds to whatever has lagged, which is the discipline rotation requires, executed without a forecast. It also gives you a rule to follow when your instincts are shouting the opposite.

body.title: What Drift Does to Your Weights
body.prompt: You start with ₹5,00,000 in a cyclical sector fund and ₹5,00,000 in a defensive sector fund, a 50:50 split. Over a year, the cyclical fund gains 40% and the defensive fund falls 10%. What percentage of your portfolio is now in the cyclical fund? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Cyclical fund: ₹5,00,000 × 1.40 = ₹7,00,000. Defensive fund: ₹5,00,000 × 0.90 = ₹4,50,000. Total = ₹11,50,000. Cyclical weight = 7,00,000 ÷ 11,50,000 = 60.9%. Without doing anything, your portfolio has become significantly more cyclical, right after cyclicals have run up. Rebalancing back to 50:50 would mean selling about ₹1,25,000 of the winner and buying the laggard. Do check the tax and exit load implications before rebalancing.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: Dividing a sector index by a broad market index such as the Nifty 50 gives a measure of ___ strength, which shows whether the sector is gaining or losing ground.
body.explanation: Relative strength strips out the overall market move and isolates leadership, which is what rotation is about.

body.title: Reading the Cycle Without Guessing
steps: Identify the current phase using rate direction, GDP growth trend, inflation, and credit growth rather than market commentary
Plot relative strength for three or four major sector indices against the Nifty 50 over one and three years
For any sector you are considering, compare current margins with their ten-year average to judge where earnings sit in the cycle
Compare current valuations with the sector's own history, using normalised earnings for cyclicals
Check the supply side: capacity expansions and new entrants usually mark late-cycle enthusiasm
Set target sector weights for your portfolio and a fixed rebalancing schedule, and write down the tax cost of switching before you act
Resist buying the top performing sector fund of the last three years without doing all of the above

points: Sector leadership rotates with the economic cycle: rate-sensitive sectors early, industrials mid-cycle, commodities late, defensives in slowdowns
Markets move ahead of the data, so leadership usually shifts before GDP or earnings confirm the new phase
Rotation is really driven by the gap between what the market expects and what a sector delivers, often starting from a low valuation
Relative strength, the sector index divided by the broad index, is the simplest way to see leadership changing
Relative return compounds: a 25% sector return against a 10% market return is 13.6% of outperformance, not 15
Rotation is far easier to see backwards than to trade forwards, and switching costs money in fees and taxes
Periodic rebalancing to target weights captures much of the discipline of rotation without requiring a forecast

body.text: The rotation map describes general tendencies, not rules, and cycles rarely repeat exactly. Chart values and portfolio examples are illustrative. Historical market descriptions are approximate and simplified. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any security or fund.
